title: Marketing strategy for a given situation
notes: Authored 2026-10-06 under standard v0.2.0-draft. All claims are provenance generated_gap, verification unverified.

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Explain why the elements of the marketing mix matter differently to consumers in given circumstances, and recommend and justify a marketing strategy that fits a stated situation.

blocks.heading: The mix and the consumer
blocks.text:
The marketing mix is the blend of four controllable elements - product, price, place and promotion - with which a business influences the customers, actual and potential, for what it sells. Topic 3.3 teaches each element in detail; this topic asks a sharper question: in a given situation, which element does the most work on the consumer’s decision?

Each element reaches the buyer through its own mechanism. The product works through fitness for the buyer’s need - a backpack that tears on the first trail fails its buyer whatever it costs. Price works through what the buyer is willing and able to pay. Place works through how easily the buyer can get the product. Promotion works through whether the buyer notices the product and knows what it offers.

blocks.heading: Which element matters most here
blocks.text: Which element most influences consumer decisions differs with circumstances, and the test is to ask which weakness would break the purchase. Take a new energy drink launched to Windhoek shoppers. Condition: nobody knows the drink, so the breaking weakness is attention - a drink no shopper notices stays on the shelf whatever it costs. Mechanism: promotion carries the launch, because tasting stands and social-media posts build the awareness the first purchase depends on. Consequence for the business: the promotion budget earns the early sales, and a price cut alone would discount a product nobody has heard of. Reverse the condition - the same drink, now well known, sitting beside three rival brands - and the breaking weakness shifts to place and price, because a shopper who knows the brand tends to take whichever tube is nearest and cheapest. The element that matters most is set by the circumstances, not by the product alone.

blocks.heading: What a marketing strategy is
blocks.text: A marketing strategy is a business’s plan for using the elements of the marketing mix together to reach a chosen target market and achieve its marketing objectives. Recommending one in a given situation means more than naming it: the recommendation has to state the choice, the circumstances that make it fit - who the target market is, what the competition is doing, what the business’s objectives and resources allow - and the criterion that decides between it and the alternatives.

blocks.heading: Recommending a strategy, with the case against
blocks.text: Kalahari Kerb runs one food truck selling spicy kapana bowls at a Windhoek taxi rank, and the lunch queue has stopped growing. The owner sees two paths: keep one truck and raise prices, or open a second truck at a petrol station on the Western Bypass and hold prices down. The facts point to a place problem: the queue is full at noon and thin after two o’clock, and social-media followers keep asking for a branch nearer their workplaces, so customers who want the bowls cannot reach them. Recommendation: open the second truck at the Bypass with the same product and the same price, because the criterion that decides is reach - the demand already exists where the truck is not. The case against: two trucks raise the running costs while the Bypass trade is untested, so the recommendation would change if a month’s trial showed the Bypass queue too thin to cover the extra costs. A New Zealand pie chain that faced the same choice rolled out one cart at a time for that reason - each site proved itself before the next opened.

blocks.heading: Two ideas often confused
blocks.text: A question about the roles of marketing is not a question about the four Ps. The roles are what marketing does for the business: identifying customer needs, satisfying them, and raising awareness of the product. The elements - product, price, place, promotion - are the controllable decisions the business blends to do those things. The test that tells them apart: ask whether the statement names a job marketing performs or a decision the business controls. A learner who answers a question about the roles of marketing with the four elements has confused the tool with the purpose, and the same confusion runs the other way when a mix question is answered with jobs instead of elements.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: Topic 3.3 teaches the four elements of the mix and how each influences sales; this topic weighs them against each other in real situations. Topic 3.2’s market research supplies the facts a recommendation needs - who the customers are and what they will pay. Topic 3.4.3 extends the same reasoning across borders: read the circumstances, recommend, and face the case against.
